name: Manila
lede: Manila is a light yellowish brown, a color name Maerz and Paul date to 1892 and shared with the Philippine capital.

sections.title: A port that moved goods
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul record Manila as a color name from 1892 [1]. The color books we hold do not explain it; they use Manila only as a place, and the port matters because of what passed through it [2].

From the 1570s Spanish galleons linked Acapulco and Manila, and that trade carried cochineal red to the Philippines and on to China, where it was called "foreign red" [2][3]. Manila also sits in the name of a dye: *Manila indigo* was the trade name for the dye of *Wrightia tinctoria*, a tree of India, Burma and Malaya [4]. One account ranks Manila indigo as the worst grade, used mainly for laundry blue [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is Maerz and Paul plate 12, C 5, which ISCC-NBS reads as a light yellowish brown [1]. It sits near [[buff]] and [[tan]] and is much paler and warmer than [[sepia]] [1]. One book mentions a manila envelope in passing, but none of ours explains the color's name, so any link to paper or rope is common usage, not something we can cite.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Manila is one of the most common colors in the ColorHub archive: it matches 2,619 paintings, about 11% of all of them, as photographed [5]. That fits a mid-tone neutral. Sargent and Catlin are among the painters who use it more than most [5].
